# The briefing and checks lists of climb batch 25's rungs (CLIMB-BATCH-25.md, section 3), made from
# plan-24/manifest/lists24.py for the batch workflow (explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/batch-redesign.md,
# "The brief"): each list holds what the rung's section cites, the decisions, the ledger rows, the notes and the code
# it rests on, and no process position or harness fact, which the brief's role text and the fortress-repo skill carry.
# POSITIONS and FACTS entries are keyed by their numbers. Each briefing entry is a pair: its facts-extract.sh key and
# one line on why it is there. A checks list is a sub-list of its briefing's keys, read by the skeptic, a repair
# round and a judge. The record's section 5, "The briefings, rung by rung", holds the same keys. No key holds a
# backslash, a backtick or a double quote, which the script refuses; facts-extract matches a heading without its
# backticks.
# The rungs, in the manifest's order, which is the gather's applied order: D, P, A, R, U, N, C (the record's fork 1).
# D, P and N have the planner's samples (plan-25/probes/sample-D.patch, sample-P.patch, sample-N.patch); A, R and U
# its whole texts (rung-A.patch, rung-R.patch, rung-U.patch); C none.
# `python3 -B lists25.py` checks every key with facts-extract.sh --check (each must match exactly one place) and every
# reason's form; it is run again on the tree the batch is cut from.

\subsection{Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators}

For most integer, rational, floating-point, complex, and interval expressions,
multiplication can be expressed using any of `\EXP{\cdot}' or
`\EXP{\times}' or simply juxtaposition.
However,
the \EXP{\times} operator is used to
express the shape of matrices, so if expressions using multiplication are used
in expressing the shape of a matrix, it may be necessary to avoid the
use of '\EXP{\times}' to
express multiplication, or to use parentheses.

For integer, rational, floating-point, complex, and interval expressions, division is expressed by \EXP{/}.
When the operator \EXP{/} is used to divide one integer by another,
the result is rational.
The operator \EXP{\div} performs truncating integer division:
\EXP{m \div n = \mathit{signum}\left({m \over n}\right) \left\lfloor \left| {m \over n} \right| \right\rfloor}.
The operator \OPR{REM} gives the remainder from such a truncating division:
\EXP{m \OPR{REM} n = m - n (m \div n)}.
The operator \OPR{MOD} gives the remainder from a floor division:
\EXP{m \OPR{MOD} n = m - n \left\lfloor {m \over n} \right\rfloor};
when \EXP{n>0} this is the usual modulus computation that evaluates integer \VAR{m}
to an integer \VAR{k} such that \EXP{0\leq{}k<n} and \VAR{n} evenly divides \EXP{m-k}.

The special operators \OPR{DIVREM} and \OPR{DIVMOD} each return a pair of values,
the quotient and the remainder; \EXP{m \OPR{DIVREM} n} returns
\EXP{(m \div n, m \OPR{REM} n)} while
\EXP{m \OPR{DIVMOD} n} returns
\EXP{(\left\lfloor {m \over n} \right\rfloor, m \OPR{MOD} n)}.

Multiplication of a vector or matrix by a scalar is done with juxtaposition,
as is multiplication of a vector by a matrix (on either side).  Vector dot product
is expressed by `\EXP{\cdot}' and vector cross product by
`\EXP{\times}'.  Division of
a matrix or vector by a scalar may be expressed using `\EXP{/}'.

The syntactic interaction of juxtaposition, \EXP{\cdot}, \EXP{\times},
and \EXP{/} is subtle.
\See{operator-precedence} for a discussion of the relative precedence of
these operations and how precedence may depend on the use of whitespace.

The handling of overflow depends on the type of the number produced.
For integer results, overflow throws an \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
Rational computations do not overflow.
For floating-point results, overflow produces \EXP{+\infty} or \EXP{-\infty}
according to the rules of IEEE 754.
For intervals, overflow produces an appropriate containing interval.

Underflow is relevant only to floating-point computations and is handled
according to the rules of IEEE 754.

The handling of division by zero depends on the type of the number produced.
For integer results, division by zero throws a \TYP{DivisionByZero}.
For rational results, division by zero produces \EXP{1/0}.
For floating-point results, division by zero produces a \TYP{NaN} value
according to the rules of IEEE 754.
For intervals, division by zero produces an appropriate containing interval
(which under many circumstances will be the interval of all possible real values and infinities).

content.content:
### 4.2 Way 2: the binding's declared types

The binding declares the Fortress types; walk already carries them so (F-299). Two places can give the checker the same reading.

**2a, in the foreign-type table** (`hard-set-way2a-table.patch`). The rewrite records each binding's declared types, `self` first and the result last, keyed by the helper's class and method; `NamingCzar` reads, at a position whose Java type carries the declared type (`int`: `NN32`, `Char`; `long`: `NN64`), the declared type in place of `ZZ32` or `ZZ64`; `ForeignJava` and the wrapper generator `FortressMethodAdapter` pass the class and the position (+85 −13 over four files).

- **What the measurements show.** `ForeignJava` reads every public method of a helper class once per JVM, at the first import of any of them, and keeps that reading (`repository/ForeignJava.java:451`, `:492`). So the reading is that of the first component whose import reaches the class. In the one library, `ZZ32`'s `unsigned` in `FortressLibrary` names `simpleUnsignedIntArith` (moved by climb batch 23), and the class was read before `FortressBuiltin`'s `NN32` `+` recorded its types: the distance 1, at that `+`, read as `(ZZ32, ZZ32)->ZZ32`. With `ZZ32`'s `unsigned` put back on its glue class for one run, and nothing else changed, the distance 0 (runs 2a-1, 2a-2). In the compiler's world, where the prelude's own `import java` reaches the class first, the sample's three bindings fail as on the base, while the wrapper that the same compile writes reads the helper at `NN32`: `javap` shows `unsignedIntOverflowingAdd(FZZ32, FZZ32)` before, `(FNN32, FNN32)` after, and `(FZZ32, FZZ32)` again after the next compile of an unrelated program (run 2a-3). Every compile that builds the foreign api writes the class's wrapper anew (`ForeignJava.java:568`; `compiler/phases/CodeGenerationPhase.java:77-94`; `compiler/nativeInterface/FortressTransformer.java:65`), and the prelude's jar calls the wrapper by its descriptor.
- **Cost.** For the 82: the patch, made order-independent, which needs every binding's types known before any class is read (a pass over the library's text before the graph, or a table written by hand, which is way 1's information kept in the checker), and one reading per helper for every user of it, the prelude's `import java` and any test's included; 82 strings. No new helper; walk no change.
- **Residue at the switch-over.** The prelude's conflict ends with the prelude; the shared wrapper and the first-reader rule stay, so a later `import java` of one of these classes at its default reading, or two bindings that declare one helper differently, break each other. No test program today `import java`s the unsigned or `Char` classes (`grep` over the test folders), and among the 213 bindings of A and B no helper is named at two declared signatures over a carried `int` or `long` (five helpers at two signatures, all among the rest: `doublePow`, `doubleCeiling`, `compareTo`, `nativeConcatenate`, `makeZZfromZZ64`).

**2b, at the rewrite, through the team's transfers** (`hard-set-way2b-rewrite.patch`). The rewrite that turns a bare body into a call of its helper (F-298) reads the declaration's type at each position; where the helper's Java type there is `int` or `long`, the stand-in table reads it as `ZZ32` or `ZZ64`, and the declared type is `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, it puts the matching transfer helper around the argument, or around the call for the result. So `opr +(self,b:NN32):NN32 = builtinPrimitive("...unsignedIntOverflowingAdd")` is checked and compiled as the prelude's text, `makeNN32FromZZ32(unsignedIntOverflowingAdd(makeZZ32FromNN32(self), makeZZ32FromNN32(b)))`. A helper that already reads a position as the declared type, as the six themselves, gets no transfer there. +86 −11 lines in `BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`, nothing else.

- **Cost.** For the 82: the patch; 80 strings, each naming the binding's existing helper (NN32's `asFloat` also needs fork 12's answer; NN32's `CHOOSE` goes through `simpleLongArith.longOverflowingChoose`, `simpleUnsignedIntArith.java:80-82`, which rung K fixes, so it follows K); no new helper; no change of the checker's table, of walk or of the code generator. `FlatString`'s `get` and `javaIndexOf` fit it too, by reading. For the rest of the 109: nothing (no carrier).
- **Residue at the switch-over.** None in the checker: the six names stay what they are now, the transfers that the prelude and the six transfer bindings already use. It binds the six helpers to staying identities: a fix of rows 856 or 857 that makes `signed` or `char` raise must bind them to new checking helpers, not change the six, which the prelude and 2b use as transfers. The compiled code makes the prelude's calls, a binary operation three wrapper calls more than one bare call; F-301 measured that C2 inlines a helper's whole path and removes the temporary box of a helper's result passed into another helper, so by reading the transfers cost nothing once hot (not measured for this composition). The rewrite runs at the parse only on the compiled path's repositories (F-298), so the composition is in no source text.
- **Measured** (runs 2b-1 to 2b-4): the distance 0; a control with two misfits, `NN32`'s `+` naming `unsignedIntLT` and `javaDigit` naming `charToUpperCase`, the distance 2, 'Function body has type Boolean, but declared return type is NN32.' and 'ZZ32->ZZ32 is not applicable to an argument of type (Char, ZZ32).', so the stage checks the composed call; walk's sample OK; walk's suite 695 tests, no failure; the compiled sample in the compiler's world, the same text that fails on the base with 3 errors, links and runs, PASS.

## 6. The three principles

- **The team's later word** (P-26: "The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text"). The compiled path's device, 2011 to 2012, is the type group's later word on a native over `NN32`, `NN64` or `Character`: two transfer helpers per type with special names, every operation's helper over the plain `int` or `long`, and the composition at the binding, with Steele's words against special names that one might "stumble across" and his hope that the compiler open-codes the transfers (section 3). It points to 2b and 3, and away from way 1's 76 new special names; its one line for a general mechanism ("should be generalized") was never acted on by the team. It says nothing on where the composition is written, by hand or by the compiler. The interpreter's bindings over these types cannot be dated: `git blame` stops at the cut commit `5a68404fd` (2012-07-19).
- **The library as the team wrote it.** The one library binds each of the 82 in one bare body at its declared types, which walk's glue carries in `int` and `long`; it holds the six transfers as public methods. It points to 1, 2a and 2b, which keep the 82 bodies as written, and away from 3, which rewrites them; P-58 takes this form ("it keeps that form").
- **What peer languages do where the team is silent.** Foreign-function declarations that name a primitive by a string and give their types in the declaration take those types as the claim and generate the conversion: OCaml's `external f : int -> int = "c_f"`, Haskell's `foreign import ccall "f" f :: Word32 -> Word32` (Haskell 2010 Report, chapter 8, marshallable foreign types), Rust's `extern "C"`, C#'s `DllImport`; that is way 2, with the conversion generated as in 2b. JVM languages that put unsigned types over signed carriers write the conversions in library source and let the compiler erase them, as Kotlin's `UInt` value class over `Int`; that is way 3. Languages that read a callee's richer types read them from metadata, Kotlin's `@Metadata` and Scala's signatures, or from the callee's own declaration, Swift's import of C's `unsigned int`; none types a callee by a substring of its name. The team is not silent here, so the peers corroborate and do not decide.
- **Where they point.** For the 82 the first two meet only at 2b; the peers' FFI practice is 2b's. For the rest of the 109 the team's prelude declared the shifts over `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` only, the library over `AnyIntegral` with the conversion inside its glue; no principle says where the conversion of an `AnyIntegral` goes once the glue goes, and the peers split (FFI marshalling, or library source).

## 7. Recommendation

**The probe's recommendation, not a decision of the curator:** way 2 at the rewrite (2b) for the 82, the 80 of them that wait on nothing else as a rung H of climb batch 24 changing only `compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java` and the 80 strings, with way 3 measured as the fallback for the rest of the 109 pending Q2 and Q3.

## 8. Decisions not taken

- **Q1. Which way for the 82.** Sources: the team's device and words (section 3; `c2c769094`, 2011-06-24; `b22c4ac56`, 2012-01-03), the library as written, P-58 (the bare form) and F-299 (walk carries by declaration). Ways: 1, 2a, 2b, 3 (section 4), with their changes. Every way keeps walk's behaviour: walk's code is unchanged in all four, and the sample's values hold on every code state (section 5). No default on record; the probe recommends 2b. Whether the principles' agreement makes this the coordinator's call or the curator's is for the coordinator: 2b chooses the compiled path's reading of every helper over these types, and is reversible.
- **Q2. The rest of the 109** (`AnyIntegral` 7, `Float` 5, `RR32` 2, `Int` 1, `FlatString`'s `=` and `flatConcat`, `Object` 2, `SEQV` and `random`, `IntLiteral` 4): a converting declaration in the library (way 3, measured for `LSHIFT`), new helpers (N3), new carriers with conversions in walk's loader and the wrapper, or the glue classes kept until a later batch. Sources: the one library's api over `AnyIntegral` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:473-474`), the prelude's shifts over `ZZ32` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:736-737`), walk's `Int.shiftCount`. Keeping the glue keeps today's behaviour. No default on record.

## The principle for the batches

Every batch lands with the specification, the library and both paths agreeing. So the work is grouped by what has to change together, not split finer.

Two rules of the batch machinery shape the order: two rungs in one batch may not change the same declaration, and a rung cannot build on another rung of its own batch, since every rung branches from the batch's base (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:465`, batch rule 1). That is why the wrapping operators and the flattening sit in different batches, and why rung O's check follows the operators.

--- XXXZZ64RemainderByZeroWalk
(* ZZ64's REM by zero throws DivisionByZero, which a catch sees; opr-overview.tex, section "Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators". *)
component XXXZZ64RemainderByZeroWalk
export Executable

dividesByZero(f: () -> ZZ64): Boolean =
  try
    f()
    false
  catch e
    DivisionByZero => true
  end

run():() = do
  assert(dividesByZero(fn () => widen(8) REM widen(0)), "ZZ64 8 REM 0 throws DivisionByZero; opr-overview.tex, section \"Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators\"")
end

end

  println("PASS")
end

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.

A \KWD{try} expression starts with \KWD{try}
followed by an expression block (the \emph{\KWD{try} block}),
followed by an optional \KWD{catch} clause, an optional \KWD{forbid}
clause, an optional \KWD{finally} clause, and finally
\KWD{end}.  A \KWD{catch} clause consists of
\KWD{catch} followed by an identifier, followed by a sequence
of subclauses (each consisting of an exception type followed by the token
\EXP{\Rightarrow} followed by an expression block).
A \KWD{forbid} clause consists of \KWD{forbid}
followed by a set of exception types.
A \KWD{finally} clause consists of \KWD{finally}
followed by an expression block.
Note that the \KWD{try} block and the clauses
form expression blocks and have the various properties of
expression blocks (described in \secref{block-expr}).


The expressions in the \KWD{try} block are first evaluated in order
until they have all completed normally, or until one of them completes
abruptly.  If the \KWD{try} block completes normally, the
\emph{provisional} value of the \KWD{try} expression is the value of the
last expression in the \KWD{try} block.  In this case, and in case of
exiting to an enclosing \KWD{label} expression, the \KWD{catch} and
\KWD{forbid} clauses are ignored.


If an expression in the \KWD{try} block completes abruptly by throwing
an exception, the exception value is bound to the identifier specified in
the \KWD{catch} clause, and the type of the exception is matched
against the subclauses of the \KWD{catch} clause in turn, exactly as in a
\KWD{typecase} expression (\secref{typecase}).
The right-hand-side expression block
of the first matching subclause is evaluated.  If it
completes normally, its value is the provisional value of the
\KWD{try} expression.  If the \KWD{catch} clause completes abruptly,
the \KWD{try} expression completes abruptly.  If a thrown exception is
not matched by the \KWD{catch} clause (or this clause is omitted), but
it is a subtype of the exception type listed in a
\KWD{forbid} clause, a new
\TYP{ForbiddenException} is created with the thrown exception as its
argument and thrown.
The exception thrown by the \KWD{try} block is \emph{chained} to the
\TYP{ForbiddenException} as described in
\secref{chained-exceptions}.


If an exception thrown from a \KWD{try} block is matched by both
\KWD{catch} and \KWD{forbid} clauses, the exception is caught by the
\KWD{catch} clause.
If an exception thrown from a \KWD{try} block is not matched by any
\KWD{catch} or \KWD{forbid} clause, the \KWD{try} expression completes
abruptly.


The expression block of the \KWD{finally} clause
is evaluated after completion of the \KWD{try} block
and any \KWD{catch} or \KWD{forbid} clause.
The type of this expression block must be ().
The expressions in the \KWD{finally} clause are evaluated in order until
